title: In what sense God is beyond word and name
source_text: Ὁ μὲν οὖν Κέλσος περὶ θεοῦ φησιν ὅτι ἐξ αὐτοῦ τὰ πάντα, ἀπολύσας οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὅπως τὰ πάντα αὐτοῦ· ὁ δ᾿ ἡμέτερος Παῦλος „ἐξ αὐτοῦ“ λέγει „καὶ δι᾿ αὐτοῦ καὶ εἰς αὐτὸν τὰ πάντα,“ παριστὰς τὴν ἀρχὴν τῆς τῶν πάντων ὑποστάσεως ἐν τῷ „ἐξ αὐτοῦ“ καὶ τὴν συνοχὴν ἐν τῷ „δι᾿ αὐτοῦ“ καὶ τὸ τέλος ἐν τῷ „εἰς αὐτόν.“ ἀληθῶς δὲ ἐξ οὐδενὸς ὁ θεός. ἐπεὶ δέ φησιν ὅτι οὐδὲ λόγῳ ἐφικτὸς, διαστέλλομαι τὸ σημαινόμενον καί φημι· εἰ μὲν λόγῳ τῷ ἐν ἡμῖν, εἴτε ἐνδιαθέτῳ εἴτε καὶ προφορικῷ, καὶ ἡμεῖς φήσομεν ὅτι οὐκ ἔστιν ἐφικτὸς τῷ λόγῳ ὁ θεός· εἰ δὲ νοήσαντες τὸ „ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεὸν, καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος“ ἀποφαινόμεθα ὅτι τούτῳ τῷ λόγῳ ἐφικτός ἐστιν ὁ θεὸς, οὐ μόνῳ αὐτῷ καταλαμβανόμενος ἀλλὰ καὶ ᾧ ἂν αὐτὸς ἀποκαλύψῃ τὸν πατέρα, ψευδοποιήσομεν τὴν Κέλσου λέξιν φάσκοντος· οὐδὲ λόγῳ ἐφικτός ἐστιν ὁ θεός. καὶ τὸ οὐκ ὀνομαστὸς δὲ διαστολῆς δεῖται. εἰ μὲν γὰρ, ὅτι οὐδὲν τῶν ἐν λέξεσι καὶ σημαινομένοις δύναται παραστῆσαι τὰς ἰδιότητας τοῦ θεοῦ, ἀληθές ἐστι τὸ λεγόμενον, εἴ γε καὶ πολλαὶ ποιότητες οὐκ εἰσὶν ὀνομασταί. τίς γὰρ δύναται ὀνόμασι διαφορὰν δοῦναι ποιότητος γλυκύτητος φοίνικος καὶ γλυκύτητος ἰσχάδος; τίς δὲ ὀνόματι δύναται διαστείλασθαι καὶ παραστῆσαι τὴν ἑκάστου ἰδίαν ποιότητα; οὐδὲν οὖν θαυμαστὸν, εἰ οὐκ ἔστιν οὕτως ὀνομαστὸς ὁ θεός. εἰ δὲ τὸ ὀνομαστὸν λαμβάνεις καθὸ οἷόν τε ἐστὶν ὀνόμασι παραστῆσαί τι τῶν περὶ αὐτοῦ εἰς τὸ χειραγωγῆσαι τὸν ἀκροατὴν καὶ ποιῆσαι νοῆσαι περὶ θεοῦ κατὰ τὸ ἐφικτὸν τῇ ἀνθρωπίνῃ φύσει τινὰ τῶν περὶ αὐτοῦ, οὐδὲν ἄτοπον λέγειν αὐτὸν ὀνομαστόν. οὕτω δὲ διαστελούμεθα καὶ τὸ οὐδὲν γὰρ πέπονθεν ὀνόματι καταληπτόν. ἀληθὲς δὲ καὶ τὸ ἔξω παντὸς πάθους εἶναι τὸν θεόν. καὶ ταῦτα μὲν ταύτῃ.
pass_a_gloss: Celsus says about God that from him (ἐξ αὐτοῦ) [are] all things, having loosed (ἀπολύω) — I know not how — all things of/from him; but our Paul says 'from him and through (διά) him and to (εἰς) him all things', presenting the beginning (ἀρχή) of the subsistence (ὑπόστασις) of all things in 'from him', the holding-together (συνοχή) in 'through him', and the end (τέλος) in 'to him'. Truly God [is] from nothing/no one (ἐξ οὐδενός). Since he says that not even by reason/word (λόγος) is he attainable (ἐφικτός), I distinguish (διαστέλλω) the meaning (σημαινόμενον) and say: if by the reason in us, whether inward (ἐνδιάθετος) or uttered (προφορικός), we too will say God is not attainable by reason; but if, understanding 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God', we declare (ἀποφαίνομαι) that by this Word God is attainable, being grasped (καταλαμβάνω) not by him alone but also by whomever he reveals (ἀποκαλύπτω) the Father to, we will make false (ψευδοποιέω) the saying of Celsus: 'nor is God attainable by reason.' And 'not nameable (ὀνομαστός)' needs distinction (διαστολή). If [meaning] that nothing in words (λέξις) and meanings can present the properties (ἰδιότης) of God, the saying is true, since many qualities (ποιότης) are not nameable. For who can give by names the difference of quality of sweetness (γλυκύτης) of a date (φοῖνιξ) and sweetness of a dried fig (ἰσχάς)? Who can by a name distinguish and present the proper quality of each? No wonder, then, if God is not thus nameable. But if you take nameable as possible by names to present something of what concerns him so as to lead by the hand (χειραγωγέω) the hearer and make [him] understand about God, as far as attainable for human nature, some of the things about him, nothing absurd (ἄτοπος) to call him nameable. Thus we will distinguish also 'for he has suffered/experienced (πάσχω, pf.) nothing graspable (καταληπτός) by a name.' True also that God is outside (ἔξω) every passion (πάθος). And so much for these.
pass_b_english: Celsus says of God that “from him are all things”, though, I do not know how, he has cut all things loose from him. Our Paul, however, says, “From him and through him and to him are all things” (Romans 11:36), showing the beginning of the existence of all things in “from him”, their holding together in “through him”, and their end in “to him”. And in truth God is from no one.

But since he says, “Nor is he attainable by reason”, I distinguish the meaning and say this. If he means the reason within us, whether held within or spoken aloud, we too shall say that God is not attainable by reason. But if, having understood the words, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1), we declare that God is attainable by this Word, and is comprehended not by him alone but also by anyone to whom he reveals the Father (Matthew 11:27), then we shall prove false the saying of Celsus, who states: “Nor is God attainable by reason.”

His “not nameable”, too, needs a distinction. If it means that nothing in words and their meanings can present the properties of God, what is said is true, since many qualities too cannot be named. For who can express in names the difference in quality between the sweetness of a date and the sweetness of a dried fig? Who can distinguish by a name and present the proper quality of each? It is no wonder, then, if in this sense God cannot be named. But if you take “nameable” to mean that it is possible to present in names something of what concerns him, so as to lead the hearer by the hand and help him grasp some things about God, as far as human nature can attain, there is nothing absurd in calling him nameable.
In the same way we shall also distinguish the saying, “For he has experienced nothing that can be grasped by a name.” And it is true as well that God is “outside every passion”. So much for this.

choices.choice: Celsus’s words quoted: ‘from him are all things’; ‘nor is he/God attainable by reason (λόγῳ)’; ‘not nameable’; ‘for he has experienced nothing that can be grasped by a name’; and, probably, ‘outside every passion’ (ἔξω παντὸς πάθους), which Origen accepts as true; the last is marked as Celsus’s phrase on the strength of the parallel ‘And this is true as well’, but the staged text gives no explicit ‘he says’. Doubtful: ἀπολύσας οὐκ οἶδ’ ὅπως τὰ πάντα αὐτοῦ, rendered ‘he has cut all things loose from him’ (Celsus gives only the ‘from him’ and leaves out ‘through him and to him’); an alternative is ‘leaving out, I know not how, the “all things are his”’. ἀληθῶς δὲ ἐξ οὐδενὸς ὁ θεός: God has no source; reviewer renders ‘God is from no one’ (οὐδενός read as masculine/neuter ‘no one, nothing’), which avoids ‘derived from nothing’ being misread as God coming out of nothing. The λόγος wordplay (reason/word vs the divine Word) cannot be kept in one English word: Celsus’s λόγος is ‘reason’, the λόγος in us is ‘held within or spoken aloud’ (ἐνδιάθετος / προφορικός, the Stoic distinction), and John’s λόγος is ‘Word’. Romans 11:36 and John 1:1 quoted verbatim. ‘Anyone to whom he reveals the Father’ is a clear allusion to Matthew 11:27 (cf. Luke 10:22). πάσχω/πάθος: ‘experienced’ for the verb in Celsus’s clause, ‘passion’ for the noun.
'God is derived from nothing' -> 'God is from no one' (ἐξ οὐδενός: God has no source; the old wording could be read as God coming out of nothing)
'not only by him alone but also' -> 'not by him alone but also' (οὐ μόνῳ αὐτῷ; removed the doubled 'only ... alone')
'make him understand some of the things concerning God' -> 'help him grasp some things about God' (removes the repeated 'concerns him ... concerning God' without losing τινὰ τῶν περὶ αὐτοῦ)
